As of 1255 AM EST Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: High pressure will remain dominant across the region 
well into the weekend, as ridging holds strong from a 1031mb high 
over SE Virginia. Dry surface air will continue to help to increase 
our high temperatures today by a degree or two from yesterday, aided 
by the lack of green vegetation. Highs today will warm to near 60 
degrees in the wider valleys and in the mid 50s for the higher 
terrain of the Adirondacks and eastern Greens. Efficient mixing from 
lowering afternoon dewpoints could lead to some additional locally 
warmer conditions, especially along the western shore of Lake 
Champlain and the greater Champlain Valley into the low 60s. Little 
change temperature wise is expected day to day towards Friday and 
Saturday due to reinforcing ridging each day. Overnight lows will 
cool into the upper 30s to low 40s west of the Champlain Valley 
tonight as warm advective winds keep temperatures elevated 
overnight. East of the Champlain Valley tonight, temperatures will 
continue to cool in the river valleys into the mid to upper 30s as 
the center of the ridge slightly shifts east. Confluent flow in the 
St. Lawrence will keep breezes between 15 to 20 mph today and into 
tonight, before subsiding late Friday.

The departing ridge late tonight will open the door for a quick 
moving moisture starved trough to sneak into the area tonight. A low 
level jet associated with the shortwave, in tandem with a tightening 
pressure gradient, will drive gusty winds above 3000ft between 30 
and 50 MPH from the Greens to the Adirondacks, respectively. As with 
past nights, these winds will be tied mainly to the summit levels as 
a steep nocturnal inversion will develop, trapping the strongest 
winds above the inversion layer, with only gusts to 15 to 20 mph in 
the St. Lawrence Valley and near Lake Champlain. Westerly winds 
Friday will increase our atmospheric moisture profiles as dewpoints 
increase into the low 40s, with above freezing dewpoints even at 
mountain summit levels. Combined with the continued breezy 
conditions at summit levels, snow melt is highly likely, with the 
potential for any and all summit level snow to melt out. Thankfully 
summit level snow depths are only around 5 inches, and therefore no 
impacts are expected for area waterways. Mid to high level clouds 
will remain through the entire near and short term period with 
clouds riding along the northern periphery of the high, with better 
chances for sunshine in our southern areas today and tomorrow. More 
areawide sunshine is likely by Saturday.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Our attention will continue to be on the development of 
surface low pressure that will have developed over the Bahamas on 
Friday moving along the US East Coast. By Sunday night into Monday, 
the system will likely be near the Mid-Atlantic shores, with 
southeasterly flow ahead of it beginning to transport moisture 
towards the New England Coast. It will be lifting north against a 
region of channeled flow from anomalous 500mb ridging in the 
Canadian Maritimes and modestly strong upper low west of Greenland. 
For our regional weather conditions, impacts will depend on how far 
west the system is located. A northern stream shortwave will get 
sheared apart within the fast southwesterly flow aloft. It will come 
out ahead of a strong upper trough swinging southeast from James 
Bay. If the coastal low is sufficiently far west, it will interact 
favorably with these northern stream features and produce a swath of 
moderate to locally heavy rain that makes it as far west as the east 
slopes of the Adirondacks and up through the Northeast Kingdom. If 
the coastal low is too far east, subsidence on its northwest side 
will make squeezing precipitation harder out of the northern stream 
system. There's still time to assess the potential, but it's 
important to note that even guidance that does track rain far 
westwards will have a coarse depiction of the precipitation shield, 
and the high res guidance will do a greater job of capturing what 
will likely be very dry air to overcome with a sharper gradient in 
forecast rainfall amounts.

After this disturbance passes east, sharply colder conditions will 
follow. We can say farewell to 50s and 60s with brisk northwest flow 
as the system ejects northeast of the region after Monday. NBM mean 
values are already depicting only upper 30s for high temperatures as 
a strong surface high builds from Tuesday through Thanksgiving Day. 
Several NWP depicts MSLP values around 1039-1043mb, which is 
certainly up there. We can expect dry weather to continue after this 
brief opportunity for some needed rain, and temperatures around 5-10 
degrees below normal heading into Thanksgiving.
